name: Subfascial breast augmentation

card.summary: A breast-implant technique that places the implant beneath the pectoral fascia, on top of the chest muscle, to add breast volume and contour while leaving the muscle undisturbed.
card.note: Elective surgery with the general risks of implants, including capsular contracture, rippling, malposition and revision surgery.

quick.overview:
Subfascial breast augmentation is a way of placing a breast implant. The surgeon makes a pocket under the thin fascia that covers the pectoralis major muscle, so the implant sits above the muscle but beneath that membrane. People choose it to increase breast size, volume and shape.

Surgeons who use the plane say the fascia adds a thin layer of extra coverage over the implant edges, and that leaving the chest muscle intact avoids the movement of the implant when the muscle flexes and the longer, more painful recovery of under-the-muscle placement. A 2020 meta-analysis of 22 observational studies found a pooled capsular contracture rate of about 1%, though the authors noted that all included studies were observational.
quick.how: It is performed by a plastic surgeon under anesthesia through an incision under the breast, in the armpit or around the areola. The surgeon lifts the fascia off the muscle, creates the pocket, and places a silicone or saline implant. Patients and surgeons often compare it with subglandular (over the muscle, under the breast tissue), dual-plane and fully submuscular placements when planning.
quick.risks: Like any breast augmentation, risks include capsular contracture (hardening of scar tissue around the implant), rippling or visible implant edges, asymmetry, malposition, infection, changes in nipple sensation and the need for later revision. Because the fascia is thin and its quality varies between people, surgeons describe the technique as dependent on anatomy and surgeon experience. Systematic reviews describe the evidence base as mostly observational.

lead: Subfascial breast augmentation is a surgical technique in which a breast implant is placed in a pocket beneath the fascia that covers the pectoralis major muscle, with the implant lying on top of the muscle itself. People use it to increase breast volume and improve contour and symmetry, and it is one of several plane options surgeons discuss alongside subglandular, dual-plane and submuscular placement.[1][2]

The technique is described in the plastic surgery literature as aiming to combine some of the advantages of the two older planes. Like subglandular placement, it leaves the chest muscle undisturbed, which proponents say avoids muscle-related pain and the implant shifting when the muscle contracts (animation deformity). Like submuscular placement, it adds a layer of tissue over the implant that can soften its edges.[2] Gould and colleagues credit Graf and colleagues in Brazil with pioneering the approach.[2]

Published research consists mainly of observational series and systematic reviews. A 2020 meta-analysis reported a pooled capsular contracture rate of about 1% across 3,743 patients, while its authors called for better-designed comparative studies.[2] In community terms the procedure belongs to the broader surgical (hardmaxx) side of appearance improvement, where it is one option among implant planes.

chain: Implant placed under the pectoral fascia, over the muscle

angle.text: The implant itself adds volume to the breast, and the fascial plane is chosen to shape how that volume looks and moves. Surgeons who favor it say it can give a natural-looking upper contour in people with enough soft tissue, such as athletic or thin patients, without the muscle movement of submuscular placement.

paras: In breast augmentation the surgeon creates a pocket for the implant in one of several planes. Wikipedia describes the subfascial approach as placing the implant under the fascia, the membrane that covers and encloses the pectoralis major, to increase breast size and volume and help with later contouring and symmetry.[1]

Gould and colleagues define the plane as lying below the prepectoral fascia and above the pectoral muscle, and note that it can be reached through an inframammary, transaxillary or periareolar incision.[2]

Subglandular placement puts the implant between the breast tissue and the muscle and is described as the plane that most closely matches the natural position of the breast, though in women with little soft tissue it is more likely to show rippling.[1] Submuscular placement, which is associated with a low capsular contracture rate, usually involves a longer and more painful recovery because of the cuts to the chest muscle, and dual-plane placement can produce animation deformity.[1] Subfascial placement was developed to reduce capsular contracture and the pain and spasm of subpectoral augmentation, while avoiding disruption of the muscle.[2]

A systematic review and meta-analysis by Gould and colleagues in Aesthetic Surgery Journal Open Forum (2020) pooled 22 studies covering 3,743 patients and found a capsular contracture rate of about 1.01%, or 0.69% in a fixed-effects model, with low heterogeneity. The authors concluded that the subfascial plane may offer low contracture rates while avoiding the discomfort and animation deformity associated with subpectoral placement, and suggested it may suit thin or athletic patients. They also noted that all included studies were observational and that follow-up and demographic reporting were inconsistent.[2]

A review of recent techniques in breast augmentation surgery notes that the field has changed substantially over roughly 70 years and that it remains to be seen how newer tools and techniques will stand the test of time.[3] A separate review of subfascial gluteal implant augmentation, a different operation in the buttock, describes subfascial placement there as a safe procedure with low morbidity in an appropriate setting.[4]

The general risks of breast implant surgery apply to any plane: capsular contracture, rippling, malposition, asymmetry, infection and the possibility of revision surgery. Wikipedia notes that animation deformity is a described risk of dual-plane placement and that rippling is more likely with subglandular placement in women with little soft tissue.[1] Gould and colleagues point out that outcome data for the subfascial plane come from observational studies and that stronger comparative evidence is still needed.[2]

The procedure is discussed mainly in plastic surgery rather than in forum communities. Within appearance-focused communities it is one of the plane choices people read about when researching breast augmentation.

timeline.event: Saline and silicone-gel breast prostheses are introduced, beginning the modern history of implant-based augmentation.[1]
Gould and colleagues publish a meta-analysis of capsular contracture in subfascial augmentation, crediting Graf and colleagues in Brazil with pioneering the approach.[2]
